title: Blue-ringed octopus
wiki_lead:
Blue-ringed octopuses, comprising the genus Hapalochlaena, are four extremely venomous species of octopus that can be found in shells between rocks and crevices in tide pools and also coral reefs in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, from Japan to Australia. They can be identified by their yellowish skin and characteristic blue and black rings that can change color dramatically when the animals are threatened. They eat small crustaceans, including crabs, hermit crabs, shrimp, and other small sea animals.
They are some of the world's most venomous marine animals. Despite their small size—12 to 20 cm (5 to 8 in)—and relatively docile nature, they are very dangerous if provoked when handled because their venom contains a powerful neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin.
The species tends to have a lifespan around two to three years, which may vary depending on factors such as nutrition, temperature, and the intensity of light within its environment.

Blue-ringed octopuses, comprising the genus Hapalochlaena, are four extremely venomous species of octopus that can be found in shells between rocks and crevices in tide pools and also coral reefs in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, from Japan to Australia. They can be identified by their yellowish skin and characteristic blue and black rings that can change color dramatically when the animals are threatened. They eat small crustaceans, including crabs, hermit crabs, shrimp, and other small sea animals.
They are some of the world's most venomous marine animals. Despite their small size—12 to 20 cm (5 to 8 in)—and relatively docile nature, they are very dangerous if provoked when handled because their venom contains a powerful neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin.
The species tends to have a lifespan around two to three years, which may vary depending on factors such as nutrition, temperature, and the intensity of light within its environment.


Classification
The genus was described by British zoologist Guy Coburn Robson in 1929. Four species of Hapalochlaena are confirmed, with six possible but still undescribed species being researched:

Greater blue-ringed octopus (H. lunulata)
Southern blue-ringed octopus or lesser blue-ringed octopus (H. maculosa)
Blue-lined octopus (H. fasciata)
H. nierstraszi was documented and described in 1938 from a single specimen found in the Bay of Bengal, with a second specimen caught and described in 2013.


Behavior
Blue-ringed octopuses spend most of their time hiding in crevices while displaying effective camouflage patterns with their dermal chromatophore cells. Like all octopuses, they can change shape easily, which allows them to squeeze into small crevices. This, along with piling up rocks outside the entrance to their lairs, helps safeguard them from predators.

If they are provoked, they quickly change color, becoming bright yellow with each of the 50–60 rings flashing bright iridescent blue within a third of a second, as an aposematic warning display. In the greater blue-ringed octopus (H. lunulata), the rings contain multilayer light reflectors called iridophores. These are arranged to reflect blue–green light in a wide viewing direction. Beneath and around each ring are dark-pigmented chromatophores that can be expanded within one second to enhance the contrast of the rings. No chromatophores are above the ring, which is unusual for cephalopods, as they typically use chromatophores to cover or spectrally modify iridescence. The fast flashes of the blue rings are achieved using muscles that are under neural control. Under normal circumstances, each ring is hidden by contraction of muscles above the iridophores. When these relax and muscles outside the ring contract, the iridescence is exposed, thereby revealing the blue color.

grok_lead: The blue-ringed octopuses (genus Hapalochlaena) are a group of small, highly venomous cephalopods renowned for their distinctive iridescent blue rings that become vividly apparent when the animal is threatened or hunting, serving as a warning display to potential predators. These octopuses typically measure 4â6 cm in body length with arms extending up to 10 cm, featuring a soft, sac-like body covered in papillae for camouflage, eight sucker-lined arms, and pale brown to yellowish skin that blends into sandy or rocky substrates. Native to the Indo-West Pacific region, they inhabit shallow coastal waters from intertidal tide pools and seagrass beds to depths of up to 50 m, often hiding in crevices, discarded shells, or algae during the day and emerging nocturnally to forage. Despite their diminutive size and reclusive nature, they rank among the most toxic marine animals due to their production of tetrodotoxin, a potent neurotoxin generated by symbiotic bacteria in their salivary glands, which can paralyze prey and pose a lethal risk to humans even from a painless bite. Comprising four recognized speciesâsuch as the greater blue-ringed octopus ( Hapalochlaena lunulata), the southern blue-ringed octopus ( H. maculosa), the blue-lined octopus ( H. fasciata), and the northern blue-ringed octopus ( H. tumida)âalong with up to around ten additional candidate species based on recent genetic studies (as of 2023), these octopuses exhibit remarkable adaptations for survival in predator-rich environments. Their geographic range spans from the Sea of Japan southward to southern Australia and westward from the Philippines to Vanuatu and Sri Lanka, thriving in temperate to subtropical reefs and rocky intertidal zones. As ambush predators, they primarily target small crustaceans like crabs and shrimp, as well as fish, using their beak to inject venom that rapidly immobilizes victims while the octopus remains unaffected due to its immunity. Blue-ringed octopuses are short-lived, with a lifespan of about one year, during which they reproduce semelparously: males use a specialized arm to transfer spermatophores to females, who then brood 50â100 eggs for around 30 days without feeding, often perishing shortly after the well-developed hatchlings emerge and disperse. Though shy and non-aggressive toward human sâbiting only when provoked or handledâtheir venom lacks an antivenom, causing respiratory paralysis that has led to at least three recorded human fatalities. Unlike the nautilus, axolotl, lobster, crab, and squid, which lack lethal venom and are not known to kill humans in typical encounters, the blue-ringed octopus can kill humans via its potent tetrodotoxin venom, which induces rapid paralysis and respiratory failure, underscoring the need for caution in their habitats. These cephalopods exemplify the ocean's hidden dangers, combining exquisite camouflage and intelligence with extreme toxicity in one of the smallest packages.
